articles.title: Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars

paras.en: Astronautsâ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars

- A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet.

A journey to Mars may be less challenging for the human heart than scientists once feared. A new study suggests that astronauts can adapt remarkably well to months of weightlessness, offering encouraging evidence that humans could endure the long trip to the Red Planet and function under its weaker gravity.

Researchers from Northwestern Medicine, UT Southwestern, and UT Houston monitored the hearts of 13 astronauts who spent approximately six months aboard the International Space Station. Their findings showed that although spaceflight initially affected heart performance, the astronauts gradually adapted, with intensive daily exercise playing an important role in maintaining their cardiovascular health.

One of NASA's major concerns about sending humans to Mars is how astronauts' hearts and circulatory systems will respond when they leave the weightless conditions of spaceflight (known as microgravity) and encounter Martian gravity, which is only about one-third as strong as Earth's.
Encouragingly, the researchers found that the astronauts showed no significant signs of cardiovascular strain when exposed to simulated Martian gravity after returning to Earth.

"With our findings, there is now reason to think that we would be able to traverse to Mars, get there and actually work on the surface of Mars," said study senior author Dr. James Thomas, professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
The study, published last month in the journal Circulation, is the first to investigate how the heart responds to simulated Martian gravity following an extended period in space.
How Daily Exercise Protects Astronauts' Hearts in Space

Living without gravity creates unusual challenges for the human body. On Earth, the heart constantly works against gravity to circulate blood, while muscles must support the body's weight. In space, those demands decrease substantially, allowing muscles and even the heart itself to shrink over time.

Returning to a gravitational environment can also be difficult. Astronauts on previous missions have frequently experienced dizziness or lightheadedness when standing after landing. This happens because gravity pulls blood toward the lower body, sometimes causing blood pressure to drop suddenly. The condition is called orthostatic hypotension. (If you've seen Sandra Bullock crawling after returning to Earth in "Gravity," you get the idea.)
However, the astronauts involved in the new study generally handled this transition well, potentially because they had maintained demanding exercise schedules throughout their missions.

As part of NASA's Exercise Countermeasures program, astronauts exercised for up to two hours each day. Their routines included 30 to 45 minutes of endurance training, which strengthens the cardiovascular system, along with 60 to 75 minutes of resistance training to help preserve muscle mass and strength.

"You lose muscle mass and cardiac mass when you're in a weightless environment because you are working less up there," explained Thomas, who also is a Northwestern Medicine cardiologist. "You're floating around in the air, and you give a little tap with your foot, and you can sail over to say hello to your buddy."
"To counter that, exercise is crucial when you're in space," Thomas added.
Heart Scans Reveal How the Body Adapts to Weightlessness

To understand what happens to the heart during prolonged spaceflight, the researchers collected echocardiograms before, during, and after each astronaut's mission. These ultrasound scans use sound waves to produce moving images of the heart, allowing doctors to examine its structure and measure how effectively it pumps blood.

While aboard the International Space Station, astronauts were trained to perform these scans on one another every few weeks. The recordings were transmitted to Earth, where researchers could monitor changes in heart function throughout the missions.
Thomas worked alongside Dr. Benjamin Levine of UT Southwestern Medical Center and Dr. Michael Bungo of the McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.

"It would be typically about 3 a.m. for me because the space station runs on Greenwich Mean Time," Thomas said. "I would watch the recordings come in live and coach the astronauts in real time to improve the images."

The scans revealed that the astronauts' hearts initially struggled to adjust to their new environment. During the first two weeks in space, researchers observed declines in cardiac filling, stroke volume, and several other measures of cardiovascular performance.

Cardiac filling refers to how much blood enters the heart between beats, while stroke volume describes the amount of blood pumped out with each contraction. Both measurements decreased early in the missions, indicating that the astronauts' hearts were temporarily moving less blood with each beat.
As the astronauts spent more time in space, their cardiovascular systems adapted. Cardiac filling and stroke volume gradually improved, approaching the levels recorded before launch.
These results suggest that the heart can adjust to prolonged weightlessness more effectively than early measurements might indicate, particularly when astronauts maintain regular physical activity.
Astronauts' Hearts Pass a Simulated Mars Gravity Test

The researchers also wanted to answer a particularly important question for future Mars missions: What happens when an astronaut who has spent months in weightlessness suddenly encounters gravity again?

Mars has roughly 38% of Earth's surface gravity. Although this is considerably weaker than what people experience on Earth, it would still force astronauts' hearts to work differently after months of floating in space.
To reproduce some of these effects, the researchers conducted a simulated Martian gravity test after the astronauts returned to Earth.
Each astronaut was tilted upward by 22 degrees from a lying position. This posture caused blood to shift toward the lower body, approximating the circulatory effects of Martian gravity.

The results were encouraging. After spending about six months in space, the astronauts' hearts performed just as well under simulated Martian gravity as they had when standing upright on Earth before their missions.

This suggests that astronauts who maintain their cardiovascular fitness during spaceflight may be capable of transitioning to the weaker gravity of Mars without experiencing major cardiovascular difficulties.
Although the findings come from a relatively small group of astronauts and a simulation rather than an actual Mars landing, they provide valuable evidence for planning future missions.

Combined with the benefits of daily exercise, the heart's ability to adapt to weightlessness and respond well to simulated Martian gravity offers another reason to be optimistic about sending humans to the Red Planet.

The study is titled "Impact of Prolonged Spaceflight on Cardiac Structure and Function: An Exploratory Longitudinal Observational Study." articles.title: Orionid meteor shower peaks tonight: Here's the best time to spot shooting stars
articles.author: Anthony Wood

paras.en: Don't miss the Orionid meteor shower peak tonight (Oct. 21-22) as tiny shards of Halley's Comet collide with Earth's atmosphere to carve fiery streaks through the Autumn sky! But will the light cast by the waxing gibbous moon spoil the show?

The Orionid meteor shower activity peaks when Earth travels through the densest section of the debris trail left by Comet 1P/Halley. The comet is currently racing back towards the sun ahead of its next visit to the inner solar system in 2061.

Under perfect dark sky conditions 10 to 20 shooting stars could brighten the night sky each hour as the peak unfolds, according to NASA. However, the light cast by the waxing moon — just four days from being full — will likely reduce the number of visible meteors by hiding fainter Orionids from sight.

Orionid shooting stars will appear to travel away from a point of origin, close to the red star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion, rising above the eastern horizon an hour before midnight for viewers in the U.S.
When and where to see Orionid shooting stars this October

Your best chance at spotting the fast-moving meteors will come in the hours before dawn on Oct. 22, after the moon has set and the radiant approaches its highest point in the night sky. It's best not to stare directly at the radiant, where the glowing meteor trails will be relatively short compared to those left by shooting stars that appear 45-90 degrees away from the bright star Betelgeuse, thanks to an effect known as foreshortening.

Try to travel away from city lights and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to adapt to the dark. Always make sure someone knows where you're going if you head somewhere remote to catch the shower and be sure to take a red light to ensure that you can find your way while also preserving your night vision!

Editor's Note: If you would like to share your Orionid shooting star photos with Space.com's readers, then please send your image(s), along with your name, location and comments to spacephotos@space.com.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

articles.title: Sci-fi legend Alan Dean Foster on his new futuristic adventure 'Lost On Paradise': 'It's paradise until you get there, and then maybe you mess it up' (interview)
articles.author: Jeff Spry

paras.en: Few names in the science fiction literary world carry as much weight and respect as author Alan Dean Foster. His award-winning 55-year career as a grandmaster of the genre continues with his latest novel from Blackstone Publishing, "Lost on Paradise", and we have an exclusive excerpt to share with our readers ahead of its release this week.

Foster famously ghost-wrote the first "Star Wars" novelization for George Lucas in 1976 and "Splinter of the Mind’s Eye" in 1978, which was intended to be a low-budget Star Wars sequel should the space opera not become a hit. He’s been a mainstay for go-to fantastic adventures featuring engaging characters, dynamic plotlines, and imaginative worlds for six decades.

In addition to crafting the screen story for "Star Trek: The Motion Picture," Foster also wrote the novelizations for the first three "Alien" films, Disney's "The Black Hole," John Carpenter's "The Thing," "The Last Starfighter," "Star Trek," "Transformers," "Terminator: Salvation", and many more.
New York Times bestselling author Alan Dean Foster, master of both action and emotion, reveals a world where everything is perfect, but nothing is as it seems…

The near-future, off-world escapades of "Lost On Paradise" are the latest addition to Foster’s acclaimed bounty of bestselling standalone novels and series, including the popular "Spellsinger" series.

"Earth is crowded, polluted, and dismal," states the novel's synopsis. "Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina scrape by on her poorly paying job and what little money he gets selling items scavenged from rich people’s trash. Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina dream of Paradise.

"Paradise: a beautiful, clean, verdant world where three races live in harmony—at least, according to the videos sent back to Earth. There are the Eiquan, masters of astonishing technology; the Lusanata, hunters and farmers; and humans, who may be restricted to a few scattered settlements, but still live a life ten times better than those on Earth.
"On the run after a criminal act, Jonos and Liina finally escape to Paradise. It's everything they hoped for. Until tragedy strikes."
The genesis of Foster's "Lost on Paradise" is something that’s been percolating in his fertile mind for many years.

"I had this notion of a planet called Paradise where everything is perfect, and everything on Earth is seriously messed up," Foster tells Space. "There’s this couple who have problems; they’re poor like everybody else.

"And you have a unique male protagonist because he recognizes that his female partner is smarter than him, so she’s the brains of the outfit, and he supplies the muscle. Although he's not stupid. Too often you get a big, hulking guy with no brains. But she has a potentially fatal disease, and they’re trying to get away like a lot of poor people in the world today. So here's a place called Paradise. How do you get there? It’s expensive and difficult. And what happens if they do? Maybe Paradise isn’t always Paradise."

paras.en: In crafting a deteriorating New York some 150 years or so down the calendar, it was important to stay sharp regarding developments that pop up in the news to avoid any internal logic conflicts.

"You just don’t want to get caught out by a scientific development that you postulate is near future when it's actually contemporary," explains Foster. "So I was very careful with that. But as you’re building out an alien environment and one that’s supposed to be perfect and beautiful, and then there’s maybe some things about it that aren’t, what do you introduce to show that?

"You don’t want to contradict yourself when you’re worldbuilding. That's a large problem that’s unfortunately common in science fiction," notes Foster. "Where somebody is breathing air, and suddenly they’re breathing methane, and it just doesn’t work. There’s a lot of different variables that come together that prove that Paradise is Paradise in some ways and not in others. A good example would be when the first Europeans reached Tahiti. The problem was that the people who entered this Paradise brought venereal disease and smallpox, to which the Polynesians had no resistance. So it's Paradise until you get there, and then maybe you mess it up."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Now enjoy our exclusive chapter excerpt from Alan Dean Foster’s "Lost On Paradise." Published by Blackstone Publishing.

Why shouldn’t a man and a woman in his and Liina’s position try to get to Paradise? Jonos mused as he treaded his way homeward. Though morning continued its ascent, the sun did not. Or so it seemed, when the omnipresent pollution often rendered day as dark as night. The gloom was useful for masking scavenging activities and for concealing one’s identity. It was less suitable for more plebian activities such as breathing and eating. Or living. Life on Earth sucked.

To emigrant humans it went without saying that Paradise was aptly named. Everyone had heard the stories. On Paradise a person could breathe freely. Without a mask, without fear of needing lung implants, without having to worry about inhaling a soupçon of strychnine or similar industrial pollutants. On Paradise food was plentiful and fresh, water devoid of contaminants. There was work, too, for anyone willing to adapt to entirely new surroundings, for those willing to acknowledge the much-talked-about overlordship of the dominant species. For arrivals willing to submit to the experimental, ever-evolving social structure, and to the limitations that were placed on newcomers, the technologically superior Eiquans professed an indifference that amounted to a willing welcome.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Or so the compendium of hugely diverse anecdotes insisted. That’s all they were, Jonos knew. Stories and speculation, rumors and conjecture. Ignoring the spotty rain that had begun to fall, he turned a corner and nearly ran over a couple who scrambled to get out of his way. The man he had accidentally jostled started to say something, quickly realized the size of the individual he was about to chastise, and mumbled on his way, dragging a woman—likely his wife—with him. Jonos paid them no mind. Half of him was engaged in navigating his way home, the other half in dreaming of what Paradise might actually be like.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In truth, he had never met anyone who had actually been to Paradise. He had never met anyone who knew anyone who had been to Paradise. That did not make the distant world any less real. The media periodically released vits and images of the place. These showed an Earth-like planet swathed in an atmosphere perfectly suitable for humans. The indigenous wildlife was fascinating, the few but thriving, improvised communities intriguing, and the rarely seen Eiquans themselves tall, gracile, and sophisticated. So what if they weren’t humanoid? They were bisymmetrical, anyway, highly intelligent, and by all accounts no worse than indifferent to the interests of other species. So beautiful and graceful was their slender physicality, so mellifluous their speech, that even though they were quite alien the idea of living among them held no fear for Jonos.

paras.en: Anything, he knew, would be a step up from Earth.

His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

paras.en: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor.

Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.)

It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. The mission ended abruptly 14 months ahead of its planned end date when scientists lost contact with the probe.

The Indian Space Research Organisation, or ISRO, had a lot riding on the success of Chandrayaan-1 moon mission, which marked the first-ever deep space mission by the Indian space agency. It was also the first mission to the moon for India, a country that hopes to launch its own crewed spacecraft and build a space station.

Chandrayaan-1 did more than just demonstrate that India's space program was capable of launching missions to the moon; it also returned some amazing science results, like evidence of water ice on the moon.

"In September 2009, scientists published results of data collected by the American M3 instrument which had detected absorption features on the polar regions of the surface of the Moon usually linked to hydroxyl- and/ or water-bearing molecules," NASA said in a mission overview.
The spacecraft carried 11 instruments to study the moon, five of them built by ISRO. The rest were experiments for the European Space Agnecy and NASA.
"In addition to the five Indian instruments, the spacecraft carried scientific equipment from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Sweden, and Bulgaria," NASA said.
It took until Nov. 8, 2008 for Chandrayaan-1 to enter lunar orbit, where it stayed until contact was lost in August 2009, most likely due to a power supply failure caused by overheating.
"This was short of the spacecraft’s planned two-year lifetime, although ISRO noted that at least 95% of its mission objectives had been accomplished by then," NASA wrote.

India did not stop at the moon with Chandrayaan-1. In 2019, the country launched the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, which carried the Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. Chandrayaan-2 reached lunar orbit successfully, but the Vikram landing failed.

The Chandrayaan-3 misson followed in 2023, which successfully landed a new Vikram lander and Pragyan rover near the moon's south pole. India plans to launch the Chandryaan-4 mission to return moon samples to Earth in 2028.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

articles.title: UARX Space troubleshoots anomalies on maiden OTV Flight
articles.author: Debra Werner

paras.en: Correction: Dawn’s Docking and Fluid Transfer Port is not a hosted payload. UARX is testing it for future refueling missions.

SAN FRANCISCO –Spanish startup UARX Space is remedying anomalies identified during the maiden flight of OSSIE-D, an orbital transfer vehicle (OTV) launched Oct. 1 aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission. At least 10 PocketQubes have been deployed.
“Immediately after launch, we experienced a communications blackout with our spacecraft,” Andrés Villa Granata, UARX co-founder and chief technology officer, told SpaceNews by email.

To fix the situation, UARX “decided to send a backup command to the OTV to enable” fault detection, isolation and recovery automation “that would deploy the payloads without ground station intervention,” Villa Granata said.

UARX sent the command to deploy payloads two days after launch “but, without reliable two-way communications with the vehicle, we didn’t know if the command was properly received,” Villa Granata said. “We made this decision to prioritize our customers’ missions in case OSSIE had more serious problems” and because we were “aware of the lifetime of the spacecraft operating on batteries.”

UARX now knows that the communications blackout was caused by “a configuration error on the interface of the Ground Station service we are using,” Villa Granata said. “The configuration was corrected, and from that point communication with OSSIE has been nominal. Since then, all spacecraft systems check outs have been performed and everything is performing nominally.”

Since communications have been restored, UARX was “able to wake up the sequencer from its ultra-low-power mode and download our deployment telemetry,” Villa Granata said. “The telemetry shows that our commands sent” two days post-launch “were received correctly. We also obtained telemetry that indicates all commanded deployments were executed correctly and the payloads were released.”
Additional payloads remain onboard OSSIE, short for Orbit Solutions to Simplify Injection and Exploration, a 200-kilogram class OTV. Some are hosted payloads.
On the flight, UARX also opted to test Dawn Aerospace’s Docking and Fluidic Transfer Port.
Others satellites on OSSIE “will be released in the future, Villa Granata said. “However, we cannot provide specific details about these customers.”
Prior to launch OSSIE-D was scheduled to deploy satellites seven and 30 days post-launch.
Some customers have posted news of their missions like German nonprofit AMSAT-Deutschland, which sent three PocketQubes into orbit on OSSIE-D.

“While the successful launch was still being celebrated in Bochum and preparations for the next planned activities were underway, a surprise announcement came in on Saturday evening, October 3,” AMSAT-DL posted Oct. 4. “We would like to inform you that we have decided to initiate the deployment sequence for the OSSIE-D payload earlier than originally planned. The deployment sequence for the deployable payloads began on October 2, 2026, at 1:48:09.950 p.m. CEST.”

Since AMSAT-Deutschland did not expect its satellites to be deployed so soon, “no one had been listening to the transmission frequencies,” the post said. “The signals from the ERMINAZ satellites went unheard at first.”

“Our three ERMINAZ-2 PocketQubes have been successfully deployed from the Picobus Deployer from Libre Space Foundation on OSSIE-D,” AMSAT-DL President Peter Gulzow told SpaceNews. “Two of our Satellites, ERMINAZ-2U and ERMINAZ-2V, are operating and under commissioning. The third one, ERMINAZ-2X status is unknown, as we have not yet been able to acquire a signal from it.”

OSSIE-D also transported PocketQubes built by the Libre Space Foundation, Orion Space of Nepal and Argentina’s National Technological University – Haedo Regional Faculty. Argentia’s National University of La Plata and Ethereal Space sent cubesats aloft on OSSIE-D.
Argentine company DIYSatellite supplied PocketQube dispensers for OSSIE-D and arranged flights for customers.

“From our side, the mission continues according to the planned timeline, and we expect our satellites to be deployed in the next weeks,” Gustavo Carpignano, DIYSatellite CEO said by email. “We will be able to assess and confirm the performance of our deployer once that deployment takes place.”
Ten OSSIE-D PocketQubes had been deployed and contacted by customers as of Oct. 15, Villa Granata said.
UARX co-founders declined to comment on the status of other satellites launched inside OSSIE-D.

Prior to the launch, UARX announced on Instagram that two three-unit cubesats from Ethereal Space were “integrated within RAMI, our CubeSat deployment system, from where they will be deployed into orbit to begin their mission.”

“Spaceflight is inherently challenging, and not every mission milestone unfolds as originally anticipated,” Ethereal CEO Shawn Cochran told SpaceNews by email. “What remains unchanged is Ethereal Space’s commitment to building a reliable, operational space-weather observing capability. We remain confident in our technology, our team, and the long-term importance of providing high-quality space-weather observations to government and commercial customers.”
OSSIE’s maiden flight was also the first demonstration of UARX deployment rings SAU&RON 24 inch and SAU&RON 15 inch.

articles.title: Summer of Quantum: Building momentum for space-based QKD
articles.author: Craft Prospect

paras.en: Glasgow, UK | 21 October 2026 – The pace of development in quantum technologies continues to accelerate, and over the past few months, space engineering company Craft Prospect has been involved in conversations across the UK, Europe, Japan and the United States exploring the future of secure communications.
Taking quantum technology from the lab to orbit

Senior Quantum Engineer Andrew Kelly presented at two key industry events this year. At the 9th Annual ScyLight Conference in Tenerife, he joined the Quantum Mission session to discuss the quantum and optical CubeSat payloads being developed for the €20 million OPS-SAT VOLT mission. The conference brought together leaders from across Europe and provided an ideal forum to discuss how emerging quantum capabilities can be integrated into future space systems.

At Newton Q 2026, Andrew presented ‘From Optical Table to Orbit: Quantum Technology for Industry and Space’, exploring the engineering challenges involved in transforming quantum research into deployable products and space-qualified systems. Discussions throughout the event highlighted growing interest in quantum communications, cybersecurity, photonics, and the infrastructure required to support future quantum networks.
As governments and industry increase investment in space and quantum technology, international collaboration is becoming increasingly important.

At SPACETIDE 2026, held in Tokyo in July, Craft Prospect Managing Director Steve Greenland participated in discussions around UK-Japan collaboration, space security, and the technologies required to build secure and resilient space infrastructure. Those conversations reinforced a clear trend: nations are actively exploring how quantum technologies work together to support future national capabilities.

Similarly, at ESA’s Quantum Technology Workshop in July, Quantum Technology Lead Natalie Pearson and Sales Engineer Rory Ireland engaged with organisations from across the European space sector, discussing emerging technologies and exploring opportunities for future collaboration.
At SmallSat 2026 in Salt Lake City in August, the conversation moved from future concepts to practical implementation.

As part of Craft Prospect’s activities throughout the conference, Head of Engineering Kevin Quillien presented work on The Quantum CubeSat, while Head of Commercial Hina Khan and AI Lead Lucy Donnell showcased progress on OPS-SAT VOLT alongside partners Bright Ascension.
The response highlighted significant interest in missions capable of demonstrating secure communications, optical networking, autonomy, and quantum-enabled technologies in orbit.
View Craft Prospect’s Quantum CubeSat poster here.
Rising demand for demonstration platforms
Across every event, one message was consistent: organisations want to move beyond theory and begin testing quantum technologies in realistic operational environments.
That growing demand is one of the drivers behind Craft Prospect’s development of a new Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) Space Network Emulator.

The platform is designed to provide a practical environment for demonstrating, integrating, and testing QKD technologies before deployment, helping industry, researchers, and mission teams reduce risk and accelerate development.
As momentum continues to build around secure communications and quantum networking, facilities that enable rapid experimentation and validation are becoming increasingly important.

A recurring theme across every event was the growing convergence of quantum technologies and space systems. As optical communications, quantum-secure networking, QKD and intelligent autonomous platforms mature, they are becoming key enablers of the next generation of Smart Secure Space.
With quantum technologies increasingly moving from research to deployment, Craft Prospect continues to develop the capabilities needed to support more secure, resilient and intelligent space systems.
Ready to accelerate your journey to quantum-secure communications?
Craft Prospect’s QKD Space Network Emulator helps organisations explore secure communication architectures, validate quantum technologies and de-risk future missions.
For enquiries about the QKD Space Network Emulator, quantum technologies, or potential collaboration opportunities, contact intelligence@craftprospect.com

articles.title: Solstar provides Wi-Fi connectivity for NASA proximity operations demonstration
articles.author: Debra Werner

paras.en: SAN FRANCISCO – Wi-Fi technology from Solstar Space connected NASA’s R5-S10 cubesat with Momentus’ Vigoride-7 orbital service vehicle during proximity operations and relayed data to NASA’s Johnson Space Center, Solstar announced Oct. 20.

The mission gave Solstar “real-world experience satisfying customers,” Solstar founder and CEO Brian Barnett told SpaceNews. “After three previous spaceflights and more than 10 years of work, what has emerged is a commercial product.”

During approximately 30 minutes of proximity operations, Solstar’s Deke Space Communicator sent more than 2,300 files including optical, infrared and lidar data collected on orbit to project leaders at NASA Johnson through an experimental data-relay link provided by Iridium Communications.

“One of the most exciting aspects of this mission is the opportunity to experiment with how Iridium’s constellation can support new types of on-orbit operations,” Ethan Haase, Iridium vice president government solutions, said in the news release. “By putting that connectivity to work in a proximity operation demonstration with Solstar, we can gain valuable insight into its potential role in future missions.”
The NASA mission also provided extensive data that be used to train artificial intelligence models for future autonomous missions including proximity operations, Barnett said.

To establish communications between spacecraft, NASA‘s Wi-Fi-enabled cubesat connected with Solstar’s Deke Space Communicator on Vigoride-7. In tests conduction on the ground prior to launch, the communications link between the NASA cubesat and Deke extended more than 200 meters.

“We are proud of the strategic partnership with Solstar and the excellent results of our work together,” Momentus CEO John Rood said in the news release. “Solstar added an important communications dimension to this mission, expanding the capabilities validated during proximity operations. Bringing together interoperable technologies expands what is possible on orbit and accelerates the development of a more connected space environment.”

Wi-Fi enabled payloads can remain in constant contact with ground controllers, Barnett said. “If we’re talking about manufacturing, satellite servicing or lunar operations, you need this capability to be in touch with your equipment 24/7.”

“We are proud to work alongside NASA, Momentus and Iridium to demonstrate a new level of connectivity for spacecraft operating in close proximity,” Barnett said in the news release. “This important program shows how Solstar’s technology can help spacecraft stay connected and deliver critical mission data in near real-time to flight controllers, space operators and mission operations engineers, laying the groundwork for more capable and coordinated activity in space.”
In June, Encore Technologies Corp. announced a $1 million investment in Solstar.
“That investment is further validation of what we’re building as Solstar moves into its next stage of growth,” Encore Technologies said in a statement.

articles.title: NASA Conducts RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions
articles.author: LaToya Dean

paras.en: NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi.
Test teams fired the developmental engine for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket.
During the test, operators also fired the engine up to the 111% power level, matching the thrust needed for new production engines to launch the SLS rocket and the Orion spacecraft to orbit.

The main objectives of the test were to acceptance test RS-25 flight components for future Artemis missions and validate the new thermal protection system, which protects the RS-25 engine nozzle from the thermal environment surrounding SLS during launch.

While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability.
Four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket for each Artemis mission.
All RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions.

articles.title: Faster to Science: A Letter to the Science Community

paras.en: NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall, from NASA Headquarters, to explain our new Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), and answer your questions.

We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long. It has taken years to move mission concepts through the current two-step process. This has often come with contract management challenges, unpredictability, and not enough funding. NASA is committed to doing better — and I’m excited to share with you how we’re making it happen.

I am so pleased that NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has empowered the Science Mission Directorate to take action and make our mission selection process move more smoothly, efficiently, and effectively. The Administrator has directed us to accelerate the delivery of science, reduce the time and resources spent on long competitive processes, and focus funding on the highest-priority missions across every NASA Science division as quickly and affordably as possible. Predictability in delivering incredible science will be at the forefront of what we do.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: We are committed to getting this right. Some of these changes will take time to fully implement. We will roll them out in stages, be thoughtful about them, and refine them with your input along the way. But time is also of the essence. By streamlining how missions are proposed, reviewed, and selected, we can make meaningful change right now. That streamlined approach is Competition Model 2.0, or CM2.0, and it is how we are answering the Administrator's call to get you to science faster.

CM2.0 starts from a simple idea: compete on the science first. Proposals will be science-focused and will not require detailed engineering plans, cost, and implementation work until they are truly needed to make a decision. This frees you to spend more of your time doing science and less of it proposing how to do science.
Here is how we will streamline mission selection across our mission classes:

CM2.0 will not change how we manage our largest missions since that process has already been reformed. After the James Webb Space Telescope, NASA conducted the Large Mission Study which drew lessons from Webb and best practices from our most successful flagships into a single, documented approach for building large missions more efficiently. Flagships will continue to follow that approach, with NASA directing the overall mission to a lead NASA Center and it will then compete the science teams and instruments through targeted solicitations.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Astro-Probes, New Frontiers, and Discovery:
These missions will move to a new, accelerated two-step competition:

- Step 1 asks for just three things: a compelling science case, a science implementation plan, and a proof-of-concept mission design. That removes roughly half of the material currently required in an Announcement of Opportunity (AO) response. This allows the initial selection to focus on what matters most, the science. It also opens the door wider, because a strong idea is judged on its merits rather than on the size of the team behind it. Principal Investigators (PI) without a major university or commercial backing will get a fair consideration, and NASA PIs at any NASA Center remain eligible to respond.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: - Step 2 is a Mission Implementation Study carried out with either NASA's two Science Centers of Excellence, the Goddard Space Flight Center, or the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). NASA SMD may award an implementation study (under the management of GSFC) for New Frontiers or Discovery to JHU/APL depending on the science selected. The mission implementation study bridges pre-Phase A and Phase A by evaluating scientific merit, science implementation merit, and mission implementation merit to ensure that risks are surfaced early on rather than hidden. Down-selection to a single mission happens partway through Phase A, and the selected mission completes Phase A and then arrives at KDP-B with a matured mission implementation design. Teams that are not selected are freed from carrying concepts through the rest of Phase A on their own.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: These updates in the mission selection process will reduce time from AO to step 2 selection by up to 45 percent. This means that the original 35-months timeline will be reduced to about 19.5 months, all while having a stronger, more mature mission at the time of selection.

These missions follow the same two-step approach with an even broader field of implementing organizations, including universities and industry partners. Implementing organizations and partners will be evaluated on past performance on projects of similar complexity and cost prior to mission selection. PI-led teams can request pairing with either a Goddard or JPL implementation team at Step 1 selection, and NASA can provide Center support where it will help with procurement, contract management, or quick resolution of technical challenges. This will result again in an up to a 45 percent reduction in the selection timeline.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: SMEX, Missions of Opportunity, Earth Venture, Hosted Payloads, and Ride Shares

These missions will move to a single-step competition with a smaller review team and virtual site visits. They will also be open to a broad range of implementing organizations. The time to final selection will drop from about 32 months to about 19 months which is a reduction of up to 40 percent. Our smallest missions will be riding the momentum of a maturing commercial space economy and will move even faster. This means more missions, more often, with more incredible science at a lower cost.
Commercial Capabilities for Every Mission Type

The commercial space industry has never been stronger—and it’s only gaining momentum. Mission and implementation teams will be expected to adopt industry best practices and emerging commercial capabilities, including commercial buses, subsystems, and multi-mission operations -- wherever they offer a technical or cost benefit. No mission class is too large or too complex to benefit from the commercial industry. We will keep assessing the commercial landscape at regular intervals, building on our recent Science as a Service Request for Information.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: By competing on science first, established teams and first-time teams stand on equal footing. The best idea wins.

Great science deserves great stewardship. Rigorous cost and schedule control remains mandatory across every mission class. Phase A estimates will inform complexity and scope trades. Therefore, breaches of control thresholds will carry real consequences of up to, and including, mission termination. That discipline is how we keep the pipeline flowing for everyone.

Our NASA Centers lead the world in spaceflight experience. Therefore, by appropriately directing work at Goddard and JPL, we will save taxpayer dollars, eliminate unnecessary competition among NASA Centers, encourage collaboration, and keep critical skills thriving across the agency.

This is a moment of real opportunity. We have an administrator who is empowering us to move faster and a commercial market that is ready to help. We have NASA Centers with unmatched expertise, and a science community whose ideas expand and redefine the bounds of human achievement in the cosmos. CM2.0 brings those strengths together so that more great ideas become great missions, all while being faster and returning more science at an affordable price for the benefit of all.

NASA leads the world in discovery and innovation, but none of that happens on its own. It happens because of you. You are the reason the list of what’s "impossible" keeps getting shorter. I am so proud of what this community has achieved, and what incredible science we will continue to discover together
Thank you for your brilliance, your dedication, and your partnership. The best of NASA Science is still ahead of us, and I cannot wait to see where this journey takes us.
Nicola Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters

articles.title: Fires Char New Guinea

paras.en: New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions, including seasonally dry savannas, tropical rainforests, and lowland swamp forests. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño, fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights, closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks.

"Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems," said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. "It's a horrible situation."

According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 19, more than any other year on record at that point in the year. "Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it's very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997," said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons, the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing, vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades.

Unusually dry weather—a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns—has primed ecosystems across the island to burn. The southernmost part of Papua New Guinea, dominated by relatively fire-prone savannas and grasslands of the Trans-Fly region, went more than 90 consecutive days without rain, according to Papua New Guinea's National Weather Service. Since August, parts of the region have seen precipitation of roughly 5 to 10 percent of normal, according to the weather service's data. Local news outlets report that drought is causing crop failures, water shortages, and school disruptions.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In this normally wet part of the world, people ignite the vast majority of fires, researchers say. Crop fires, pasture maintenance, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting are all common reasons people burn in New Guinea. In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island.

"We're seeing an exceptionally high level of fire activity in Papua New Guinea and Eastern Indonesia, particularly Indonesian Papua and Kalimantan, this year compared with Sumatra and other parts of Western Indonesia," said Yang Chen, an associate researcher at the University of California, Irvine. "Papua has emerged as Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier."

Over the past two decades, land in Indonesian Papua has been cleared for industrial oil palm and pulpwood plantations, shifting small-scale cultivation, urban expansion, and mining. According to Global Forest Watch, the region lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double the 2024 total and the most since 2017.

Sumatra's fires are relatively low compared to other drought years partly because many areas are already developed. "Areas with large oil palm, sugarcane, or pulpwood plantations also often have their own private fire brigades to protect their assets," said Field. "It's in unmanaged areas or primary forest edges where we're generally seeing the most fire."
Researchers expect the fires to continue until the heavy rains of the wet season arrive in the southern part of New Guinea, typically in early November.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Aid for Ethiopia, Abyei drone strikes condemned, extreme heat and newborn health

paras.en: World News in Brief: Aid for Ethiopia, Abyei drone strikes condemned, extreme heat and newborn health

The World Health Organization (WHO) is scaling up emergency health response operations across Afar, Amhara and Tigray in Ethiopia to address growing humanitarian and health needs resulting from ongoing hostilities.

The UN health agency has strengthened its emergency coordination, deployed technical teams and expanded operational support to keep essential health services running in conflict-affected areas of the north.

Working with regional authorities, WHO is supporting preparedness, response coordination, disease surveillance and lifesaving interventions in collaboration with a range of partners, including the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the UN refugee agency, UNHCR.
WHO has delivered more than 71 metric tonnes of essential supplies to Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
Aid includes emergency health kits, cholera response materials, reproductive health kits and medicine for noncommunicable diseases.
The agency is also backing outbreak investigation, vaccine distribution and emergency referrals while strengthening public health monitoring in areas affected by insecurity and displacement.
Mobile teams and facilities continue to provide essential services, including primary care, disease prevention and maternal and reproductive health services.
Guterres deplores recent deadly attack in Abyei
UN Secretary-General António Guterres has urged authorities in Sudan and South Sudan to act to avert further attacks in the disputed Abyei border region.
The Secretary-General strongly condemned deadly drone strikes near a busy market on Monday that killed dozens of civilians, injured many others and set structures ablaze.
“I express my deepest and heartfelt condolences to the families of those who lost their lives and wish a swift recovery to the injured,” he said in a statement published late on Wednesday.

He noted that in the aftermath of the attack, the UN peacekeeping force in Abyei (UNISFA) deployed medical personnel, firefighting equipment and quick reaction forces to provide emergency treatment, support casualty evacuation and prevent the fire from spreading.

The strikes on Amiet Market and the Todach area are among the latest developments in the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that erupted in April 2023.
The Secretary-General stressed that attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure are prohibited under international law.

“I remind that all parties to the armed conflict must comply with their obligations under international humanitarian law, including to respect and protect civilians at all times,” he said, underlining the need for accountability and calling on the Governments of South Sudan and Sudan “to take all steps possible to help prevent further attacks and uphold Abyei’s demilitarised status”.
New tool tracks heat’s impact on pregnancy, newborns and children
Extreme heat can put lives at risk even before birth. It also raises health risks during pregnancy and for newborns and young children.
To help countries track these dangers, a group of UN agencies has launched the first set of priority indicators focused on these vulnerable groups.

“Our health systems need the data to recognise this reality and take action,” said Bruce Gordon, interim director of environment, climate change, One Health and migration at the World Health Organization (WHO).
That means everything from protecting people during heatwaves to building climate risk into everyday health services, he added.

WHO, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), UNICEF and the UN reproductive health agency, UNFPA, launched the new framework designed to strengthen preparedness, improve monitoring and accelerate response.
The new report recommends that countries monitor pre-term births, stillbirths, low birthweight, pregnancy hypertension, child deaths and health-facility visits during extreme heat.
Monitoring school attendance can also help reveal how heat is disrupting children’s lives.
An estimated 1.5 billion children worldwide are exposed to heatwaves that are becoming more frequent, longer or more severe.

The new information can help health governments prepare facilities for rising demand, strengthen warnings to pregnant women and families, identify communities at greatest risk and improve planning, the agencies said.

articles.title: ‘Ominous start’ to West Bank olive harvest amid settler attacks

paras.en: ‘Ominous start’ to West Bank olive harvest amid settler attacks

At least 160 Israeli settler attacks linked to the olive harvest were recorded in the first two weeks of October, according to the UN aid coordination office (OCHA) – often under the protection of, or with the participation of, Israeli forces.

Settlers have also damaged Palestinian property and stolen harvested olives and farm equipment. Last Friday, they assaulted a Washington Post photojournalist covering the harvest and the following day attacked European diplomats visiting a Palestinian community.

On Thursday, the UN human rights office (OHCHR) in the Occupied Palestinian Territory urged states and donors to go beyond condemnation and take urgent action to protect Palestinian communities as the season gets off to an “ominous start”.

Thousands of Palestinian farmers are unable to reach their olive trees because of severe Israeli movement restrictions, which have dramatically worsened over the past three years. Meanwhile, according to OHCHR, settlers are being allowed onto Palestinians’ land to harvest their crops.

“Palestinians often say that olive trees are symbolic of their existence as a group and their connection to the land,” said Ajith Sunghay, Head of the UN human rights office in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
“This is yet another tool of displacement and dispossession, adding to the suffering of communities whose rights are under attack on a daily basis.”

The toll on the olive sector has been heavy. The Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture estimates losses at $157 million since October 2023 and says 90 per cent of Gaza’s two million olive trees have been destroyed in that time.
In the West Bank, 286,000 olive trees were damaged between 2023 and the end of September 2026, including 100,000 this year, even before the harvest season began.

Mr. Sunghay reiterated a call by the Protection Cluster – a network of more than 100 international and national organisations led by his office – for Member States to increase their diplomatic field presence in high-risk communities, particularly during harvest periods.

The Cluster urged national governments to press Israel to ensure Palestinians’ safe access to their agricultural land, protect farmers from violence and expulsion, strengthen accountability and end settler expansion.
- timely and flexible funding for protective presence
Amid Israeli settler attacks across the West Bank over the years, UN agencies have a long history of taking action to protect Palestinian farmers.
Staffers with the UN relief agency for Palestine refugees (UNRWA) have helped farmers harvest olives, including in Beit Surik, Biddu and Wadi Fukin.

UN officials have also met with communities to mitigate attacks, including allocating $750,000 from the Humanitarian Fund in 2024 to support olive farmers, saying they must have unimpeded and safe access to their groves.

articles.title: Fate unknown of many returned to DPR Korea from China: UN independent experts

paras.en: Fate unknown of many returned to DPR Korea from China: UN independent experts

Three years on from the reported resumption of large-scale forcible returns of nationals of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) from China, serious concerns persist about their fate, according to a group of Human Rights Council-appointed independent experts.
There is no information on the whereabouts and treatment of those repatriated – or those who remain at risk of return – the experts said in a press release on Wednesday.

“These events form part of a longstanding pattern of serious human rights violations against individuals forcibly returned to the DPRK. In the absence of independent monitoring in either country, many returnees remain unaccounted for,” they said.

“For as long as their fate and whereabouts remain unknown, returnees are deprived of essential safeguards against enforced disappearance, arbitrary detention, execution, torture, forced labour, sexual and gender-based violence and other serious human rights violations,” the experts added.
Reports indicate that some women who left the DPRK – commonly known as North Korea – became victims of trafficking, forced marriage and sexual exploitation.
Among them is Kim Cheol-ok, who reportedly fled the DPRK during the 1990s famine and was trafficked into China as a child.
Forced into marriage at 14, she was subjected to sexual violence and forced pregnancy.
Despite living in China for about 25 years and establishing family ties, she reportedly faced harassment and restrictions due to her irregular status.
Detained by Chinese authorities in April 2023 without access to legal representation, she was forcibly returned in October 2023. Her fate and whereabouts remain unknown.
The Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found in 2024 that her detention by China and the DPRK was arbitrary.

Since 2023, reports have emerged of serious human rights violations against returnees, particularly those perceived as having sought asylum or who left the country without authorisation, raising concerns under the principle of non-refoulement.
The principle states that no one should be returned to a country where they face a real risk of persecution, torture or inhuman treatment.
“Irregular migration status does not diminish the obligation to respect the principle of non-refoulement,” the experts said.

“Given longstanding evidence that DPRK nationals who leave the country without authorisation, or seek protection abroad, may face severe punishment upon return,” they said, the reported mass returns “raise questions about whether their protection needs were adequately assessed before repatriation”.

The experts said “persistent obstacles continue to impede efforts to obtain information” on the fate and whereabouts of returnees – including those in political prison camps – as well as those who remain at risk of forcible return from China.

They called on China to respect the principle of non-refoulement, refrain from repatriating North Koreans “and ensure access to fair and effective procedures for assessing their international protection needs”.
They also called on Pyongyang to disclose the fate and whereabouts of returnees.
Special Rapporteurs and other independent experts are appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on specific human rights themes or country situations.
They serve in their individual capacity, are independent of any government or organization, are not UN staff and receive no salary for their work.

articles.title: Fernandes criticises coaches, Carrick criticises players - but who was to blame?

paras.en: Manchester United: Bruno Fernandes criticises coaches as Michael Carrick questions players after Champions League loss to Como

Man Utd were thumped 4-1 by Como in the Champions League - a result which left Bruno Fernandes criticising the United coaching staff and Michael Carrick raising the question of motivation and intensity about his players; United are on a seven-game winless run across all competitions
Who was to blame for Manchester United's miserable 4-1 defeat at Como in the Champions League?
Bruno Fernandes criticised the tactical plan of the Man Utd coaches.
Michael Carrick questioned the motivation of his players.
If only Man Utd's performance on the pitch in Italy was as forceful as the post-match interviews.

- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream Premier League games with no contract📺

After losing at Atletico Madrid last time out in the Champions League, Lisandro Martinez hit out at the club's hierarchy, calling out technical director Jason Wilcox for failings in the transfer window.
This time captain Fernandes took aim at the club's coaching staff in a stinging take-down of their pressing plan.
Asked by TNT Sports about a lack of cohesion in United's work out of possession, Fernandes defended his team-mates and put the blame on Carrick and his coaches.
"It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave a little space in behind and try to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball," he said.

"But sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confident, they have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball the legs are, and the brain, much more difficult to make it work."
Was that tactical idea what cost Man Utd in Como? "That's on the manager and on the staff to see it, it's not on me," said Fernandes.
"I just said, I think sometimes we have to be more brave on the pressure, trying to take a risk of getting that press very high and making them uncomfortable - as they did to us."

A meeting between Carrick, Martinez and Wilcox repaired relations after the centre-back's comments in Madrid. But Carrick gave a blunt response in his post-match press conference on Wednesday when Fernandes' thoughts were put to him.
"We half pressed man-to-man in the second half and ended up conceding a goal from that," he said. "Whatever tactics you play, if you don't run back, you ain't going to win."
'Angry' Carrick: You can't choose when to give absolutely everything
Carrick is usually measured in front of the media but he made his feelings clear after the club's winless run stretched to seven games with this loss.
"I'm really angry," he said. "For us to play in that way is not acceptable."
For all United did wrong in the game, it was the application of his players which was prominent in his post-match assessment.

"I'll definitely look at what we've done [as a coaching staff] or if it's the motivation and the intention and the purpose and the intensity of a game of football you have to bring," he said. "We didn't bring that today.
"You can't turn it on and off and you can't choose when you want to perform or when you don't want to perform or when you give absolutely everything or when you maybe don't," he told TNT Sports.

Carrick, who apologised after the game to United's travelling support, later added in his press conference: "It wasn't just the goals. It was the manner we went about that was the difficult thing to watch. It's not about me right now. The results can come and go, but you've got to do it in a certain way. That wasn't it."

It's now two defeats in three Champions League games this season. Fernandes, Carrick and United will have to show the solutions to their problems at home to Bournemouth on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, if their winless streak is to end in the Premier League this weekend.

articles.title: Can McLaren 'up their game' to respond to Red Bull threat?

paras.en: United States GP: McLaren with upgrades for Austin race as reigning F1 champions bid to ward off Red Bull threat

McLaren bidding to hit back with stronger results across the next triple header after seeing Red Bull close right up on them in Constructors' Championship in fight for third; watch every session of the United States GP in Austin from Friday evening, live on Sky Sports F1

McLaren will introduce further upgrades at the United States Grand Prix as they bid to improve their car's performance and stave off a resurgent Red Bull in the standings over the remainder of the season.

The reigning world champions continue to sit third in the Constructors' Championship with six rounds to go but fell into the clutches of fourth-placed Red Bull over the first of the end-of-season triple headers.

While McLaren failed to score a podium across that run of races, Red Bull claimed four top-three finishes - including two wins for Max Verstappen - to cut what had been a 76-point deficit to their rivals to just seven points.

McLaren's official pre-Austin preview described the team's results over the last three events as falling "significantly short of expectations" and that their 33-point haul in that run was "significantly lower than anticipated".
McLaren now head to a Circuit of the Americas track in Austin this weekend that they are hoping will be more suited to the strengths of their car, which will be boosted by some further revisions.

Rob Marshall, McLaren's chief technical officer, said: "We're bringing a modest selection of upgrades for this event, aimed at improving some braking reliability and performance issues. We also have some small floor changes to test.
"We have all seen how difficult it is to predict the relative performance of the top teams over the last five or six races.

"Obviously, there are many factors in play here: cars being upgraded, cars suiting and drivers liking certain circuits among other factors. The last few races have not been great for us, but I think we're getting stronger again and Austin is probably a better circuit for our car.
"Practice will be important for correlating what we've seen in our development tools with the track.
"We are still learning how best to extract performance from this car. We have the full range of corner types here so getting the best balance for the whole lap will be our main focus."

McLaren's cause in Singapore was not helped by them losing eight points on the final lap of the Sprint when their cars collided after Lando Norris attempted an overtake on Oscar Piastri. Norris later apologised for the accident, admitting it was ill-advised move on his team-mate at such a late stage of the short-form race.
The world champion said in the team's Austin preview that "I take responsibility for my mistakes, and I learn from them".

McLaren now return to the scene of a previous high-profile incident in Austin from 2025, when both their drivers crashed out on the first lap of the Sprint in a chain reaction set off by Piastri colliding with Nico Hulkenberg, and have little room for any similar missed opportunities 12 months on.
Speaking on the post-Singapore GP edition of The F1 Show podcast, Sky Sports F1's Bernie Collins said: "McLaren have had a few incidents through the year where they have not maximised their points.

"[In Singapore] Max Verstappen maximised the result, McLaren did not and there have been several weekends where McLaren did not maximise the result. This accident [in the Sprint] was a silly example of it.

"Arguably, I think if Hadjar hadn't missed three races when Liam Lawson was in that car Red Bull would be ahead of McLaren. And that's what McLaren know, that they have been saved I think, at this stage, because Hadjar wasn't in that car for three races and [Red Bull] weren't scoring the points that they could have done.
"But now Red Bull are on the up and they need to up their game if they are going to survive in that P3 position because it doesn't look like it at the moment."

Karun Chandhok added: "I think they probably know they now have the fourth-fastest car, which is a bit of a concern, and Red Bull are probably now the fastest if not second-fastest car for most tracks."
