articles.title: Premium Guard Refreshes TRICO Brand With New Identity
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Premium Guard, Inc. (PGI), a global manufacturer and supplier of automotive products and solutions, unveiled a refreshed identity for TRICO®. The updated identity preserves the recognition and equity of one of the industry’s most established names while expressing PGI’s broader vision for TRICO as a wiper and driver visibility technology platform, the company said.

For generations, TRICO has advanced driver visibility through innovation in wiping systems, winter technology, attachment systems, vehicle-specific fitment, beam blades, and advanced wiping materials. Throughout that evolution, the purpose has remained consistent: helping drivers maintain clear, dependable visibility across changing vehicles, weather conditions, and driving environments.

“We view it as a tremendous privilege to become stewards of a platform with such a deep engineering heritage,” said Anan Bishara, founder and CEO of PGI. “Our responsibility is not simply to preserve what TRICO has built, but to invest in it, expand it and use that foundation to create the next generation of driver visibility technology.”
Three Lines Represent Innovation, Engineering and Performance

At the center of the refreshed TRICO identity are its three distinctive lines, now representing three principles that connect the brand’s heritage to its future. The three-line graphic provides a visual expression of the TRICO name while giving new meaning to the principles that will guide the brand forward: Innovation, Engineering, and Performance.

Innovation reflects TRICO’s history of advancing the category through new approaches to wiping systems, winter performance, attachment technology, beam construction, and vehicle-specific replacement solutions. The introduction of TRICO Exact Fit® in 1995 is an example of that approach — recognizing early that a replacement wiper should be engineered around the specific vehicle application, connecting fitment directly with performance, PGI said.
The company intends to carry that mindset forward through investment in R&D, rubber technology, materials science, application engineering, wiping dynamics, and future driver-visibility technologies.
TRICO to Serve as Broader Technology Platform

PGI’s vision for TRICO extends beyond the TRICO-branded product line. TRICO will serve as a broader wiper and driver visibility technology platform, supporting continued innovation under the TRICO name while also helping PGI customers build and strengthen their proprietary brands and execute differentiated product strategies.

“TRICO gives PGI a powerful technology foundation,” Bishara said. “We will use it to grow the TRICO brand and to support our customers with technology and product solutions aligned with how they want to compete. That reflects PGI’s customer-first culture and our commitment to excellence and innovation.”

articles.title: Automotive Suspension Market Projected to Reach $43.2 Billion by 2033
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: The automotive suspension market will grow from $39.6 billion in 2026 to $43.2 billion by 2033, according to MarketsandMarkets. The report projects a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 1.2%. The automotive suspension market continues to expand as manufacturers transition from passive mechanical components to electronically controlled, software-coordinated systems.

Increasing adoption of adaptive and semi-active dampers and air suspension allows automakers to optimize ride comfort, handling and body control independently. These technologies reduce reliance on fixed spring-damper characteristics.

Software-defined vehicles and automated driving also increase the need to coordinate suspension with steering, braking and vehicle-motion-control systems. Suppliers such as ZF already integrate active and semi-active damping with centralized chassis software.

Larger battery packs increase vehicle mass and alter weight distribution. Growing SUV and large-vehicle adoption also increases requirements for load management, ride-height control and roll and pitch suppression. These factors support higher-value suspension architectures.

Sensor- and camera-informed predictive suspension offers another growth opportunity. These systems use road-surface information to adjust damping before vehicles encounter disturbances. For example, ZF’s AI Road Sense feeds road-condition data into chassis software to control damping in real time.

However, active and semi-active suspension systems increase complexity, sensor and actuator requirements, functional safety demands and calibration efforts. Automakers must justify higher costs through measurable improvements in ride quality, handling and safety. Scalable architectures and software reuse remain critical for mass-market adoption.
MacPherson Suspensions Expected to Maintain Largest Market Share

MacPherson struts remain the most widely adopted front-suspension architecture globally. Asia-Pacific represents the largest market by volume because of high production of compact and midsize passenger cars and light commercial vehicles (LCVs).

Low costs, compact packaging, simplified components and reduced weight make MacPherson struts suitable for high-volume vehicle platforms. Eliminating a separate upper control arm also reduces weight while maintaining adequate ride and handling performance.
Estimates indicate MacPherson struts accounted for more than 70% of compact and midsize vehicle front-suspension applications in 2025. This estimate covers China, India and Southeast Asia.

Compatibility with modular vehicle platforms allows automakers to standardize suspension layouts across multiple models. This reduces engineering, tooling and assembly complexity while supporting internal combustion engine (ICE) and electric vehicle (EV) packaging requirements.

MacPherson suspensions dominate mainstream vehicles across Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America. However, premium SUVs, performance vehicles and higher-end EVs increasingly use double-wishbone or multilink front suspensions. These advanced architectures provide greater wheel control, handling precision and ride refinement.

MacPherson suspensions retain volume leadership in cost-sensitive applications, while advanced architectures serve higher-value vehicles. Suppliers increasingly focus on higher-content MacPherson systems rather than replacing the architecture. These systems incorporate lightweight struts, integrated knuckles, advanced dampers and electronically controlled modules.
Active Suspension Projected to Experience Fastest Growth

Active suspension represents the fastest-growing suspension segment during the forecast period. Growing demand for ride comfort, handling precision, safety and real-time vehicle dynamics drives adoption, particularly among premium passenger vehicles and SUVs.

In 2025, Asia-Pacific accounted for more than 60% of new-vehicle SUV sales. Higher curb weights and elevated ride heights increase demand for adaptive and active suspension systems. High-end EVs and luxury SUVs increasingly incorporate electronically controlled suspension technologies. Examples include the Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV, Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo and BMW iX.

These systems manage battery-related mass, variable loading, pitch, roll and ride comfort. Active suspensions continuously generate counterforces at each wheel, providing greater body-motion control than passive or semi-active systems.

Integrated chassis control also supports adoption. Active suspension coordinates with steering, braking and torque-vectoring systems to manage pitch, roll, heave and wheel loads independently. These capabilities improve vehicle control during acceleration, braking and cornering.

High-performance EVs and premium SUVs require systems that compensate for greater vehicle mass and rapidly changing axle loads. Manufacturers must maintain ride comfort and handling despite these demands.
Predictive Suspension Technologies Gain Importance

Camera-based advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and road-preview technologies support predictive suspension development. These technologies detect road disturbances before wheels encounter them and proactively adjust actuator force. This shifts suspension technology from reactive damping toward software-controlled vehicle-motion management.

Integrating sensors, ADAS and software-defined vehicle platforms also enables predictive damping and load-sensitive suspension control. These developments increase the importance of software and electronic components within suspension systems.

Suppliers can differentiate their products through adaptive control, software calibration and integrated vehicle-dynamics functions. These capabilities also help premium automakers distinguish their EV and SUV driving experiences.

articles.title: PACCAR Connect to Launch in Kenworth, Peterbilt Trucks in 2027
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: PACCAR announced PACCAR Connect, a new factory-integrated platform combining telematics, driver productivity tools and fleet applications in Kenworth and Peterbilt Class 8 trucks. PACCAR unveiled the platform at the American Trucking Associations’ (ATA) Management Conference & Exhibition (MCE) in Charlotte, North Carolina. Both truck manufacturers will offer the platform beginning in early 2027.
PACCAR Connect Integrates Vehicle Functions and Fleet Applications

PACCAR Connect operates through a new touch-screen display. It pairs essential vehicle functions with an expanding suite of apps and tools for drivers and fleets. For fleets and owner-operators, the platform can eliminate the need for multiple aftermarket devices. PACCAR also covers PACCAR Connect under its factory warranty. The platform provides greater flexibility to manage fleet services.

“PACCAR Connect advances our connected vehicle strategy,” said John Rich, PACCAR chief technology officer. “By creating a future-ready technology foundation, it enables us to continuously expand capabilities, integrate new technologies and enhance the driver experience.”
PACCAR Connect provides customers access to the Virtual Vehicle software platform. The platform includes an applications marketplace that enables fleets to access a growing selection of applications.

Kenworth and Peterbilt customers can access and activate applications directly through the PACCAR Connect Portal. This allows fleets to integrate their workflows and technology directly into the truck.

The PACCAR Connect Portal provides back-office tools for fleet management. These include enhanced capabilities to monitor vehicle health, remote diagnostics, mileage, location, warranty status, idle time and more.
Kenworth and Peterbilt’s implementation includes several features specifically designed for trucks and their drivers.
- High-definition touch-screen display: Provides access to vehicle functions and applications.
- Voice assistant: Offers voice-controlled access to select truck functions and information.
- Camera integration: Supports up to eight camera inputs. Vehicle functions, including reversing and turn signals, can automatically trigger camera views.
- Bluetooth connectivity: Supports simultaneous pairing of two phones and Apple CarPlay compatibility.
- PACCAR apps: Provides drivers access to a Digital Operator’s Manual, Driver Tutorials, Vehicle Health information and a Dealer Locator.
For more information about PACCAR Connect in Kenworth and Peterbilt trucks, visit www.kenworth.com or www.peterbilt.com.

articles.title: Will Tesla's 'flying car' ever hit the market, or is it a load of compressed air?
articles.author: Kenna Hughes-Castleberry

paras.en: Flying cars once seemed like the stuff of science fiction. But Tesla's recent demonstration, which showed the company's Rocket Roadster model briefly flying, has reignited the conversation about whether flying cars could soon become a reality.

The technology behind flying cars is continuing to advance, with companies developing vehicles that combine elements of traditional cars, helicopters, electric aircraft, and — in Tesla's case — rockets. Many of these designs use electric vertical-takeoff-and-landing technology, which allows them to lift off and land without a runway by using multiple rotors or propellers to generate lift. Advances in battery technology, autonomous flight systems and computer-assisted navigation are helping to make these vehicles seem more feasible. But challenges remain, including questions surrounding passenger safety, affordability, and the need for regulations and laws and infrastructure for the widespread use of these vehicles.

paras.en: Tesla says production of its new "flying car" is scheduled for 2028, but the company is notorious for not meeting its proposed deadlines.
